claim: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) was discovered more than 30 years ago.
source: The discovery of the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) more than 30 years ago (Smith et al., 1991) triggered a wave of mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the neuronal determinants that drive inhalation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 1991

claim: The discovery of the preBötzinger complex triggered mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the neuronal determinants that drive inhalation.
source: The discovery of the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) more than 30 years ago (Smith et al., 1991) triggered a wave of mechanistic studies aimed at understanding the neuronal determinants that drive inhalation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 1991 and general scientific knowledge

claim: Exhalation begins with postinspiration or E1 phase.
source: Exhalation is traditionally subdivided into different phases – exhalation begins with postinspiration or E1 phase (Bautista and Dutschmann, 2014; Dutschmann and Dick, 2012), followed by late expiration or the E2 phase (Richter and Smith, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bautista and Dutschmann, 2014; Dutschmann and Dick, 2012

claim: Postinspiration is followed by late expiration or the E2 phase.
source: Exhalation is traditionally subdivided into different phases – exhalation begins with postinspiration or E1 phase (Bautista and Dutschmann, 2014; Dutschmann and Dick, 2012), followed by late expiration or the E2 phase (Richter and Smith, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Richter and Smith, 2014

claim: Active expiration is associated with the conditional activation of intercostal and abdominal muscles that are recruited during high metabolic demand.
source: But there is also 'active expiration' which is associated with the conditional activation of intercostal and abdominal muscles that are recruited during high metabolic demand (Abdala et al., 2009; Flor et al., 2020; Molkov et al., 2011; Pisanski and Pagliardini, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abdala et al., 2009; Flor et al., 2020; Molkov et al., 2011; Pisanski and Pagliardini, 2019

claim: Postinspiratory complex (PiCo) is located within the intermediate reticular nucleus (IRt).
source: Postinspiratory complex (PiCo) has been defined by a population of interneurons, located within the intermediate reticular nucleus (IRt) that uniquely co-expresses both glutamate and acetylcholine.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: PiCo uniquely co-expresses both glutamate and acetylcholine.
source: Postinspiratory complex (PiCo) has been defined by a population of interneurons, located within the intermediate reticular nucleus (IRt) that uniquely co-expresses both glutamate and acetylcholine.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: PiCo is both sufficient and necessary for generating the postinspiratory phase of breathing.
source: PiCo is both sufficient and necessary for generating the postinspiratory phase of breathing.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: PiCo may be involved in various postinspiratory behaviors such as swallowing and vocalization.
source: Indeed, it was hypothesized that this complex may be involved in various postinspiratory behaviors such as swallowing and vocalization (Anderson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2016

claim: PiCo serves as a relay within the IRt that integrates postinspiratory motor outputs and other non-respiratory central pattern generators (CPGs) such as swallowing, crying, lapping, and whisking.
source: This hypothesis was subsequently confirmed as work in the rat has shown this region serves as a relay within the IRt that integrates postinspiratory motor outputs and other non-respiratory central pattern generators (CPGs) such as swallowing, crying, lapping, and whisking (Toor et al., 2019; Dempsey et al., 2021; Hartmann and Brecht, 2020; Hülsmann et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2014; Pitts et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The swallow motor pattern involves coordinated bilateral activation of more than 26 pairs of muscles innervated by 5 cranial nerves.
source: The swallow motor pattern involves coordinated bilateral activation of more than 26 pairs of muscles innervated by 5 cranial nerves to ensure proper food/liquid breakdown (oral phase), safe transfer of the bolus (pharyngeal and esophageal phase) to the stomach, and airway protection (Matsuo and Palmer, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matsuo and Palmer, 2008

claim: Swallow motor pattern moves spatiotemporally in a rostral to caudal direction: starting with the oropharynx and ending with the upper and lower esophageal sphincters.
source: Swallow motor pattern moves spatiotemporally in a rostral to caudal direction: starting with the oropharynx and ending with the upper and lower esophageal sphincters (Doty and Bosma, 1956; Pitts and Iceman, 2023; Thexton et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doty and Bosma, 1956; Pitts and Iceman, 2023; Thexton et al., 2007

claim: The submental complex includes mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and digastric muscles innervated by the trigeminal, hypoglossal, and facial nerves, respectively.
source: While this study focuses primarily on the pharyngeal phase of swallow, we record swallow behavior from muscles of the oropharynx deemed 'submental complex' including mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and digastric muscles innervated by the trigeminal, hypoglossal, and facial nerves, respectively (Erik Van Lunteren, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erik Van Lunteren, 1988

claim: Muscles of the laryngopharynx include thyrohyoid, posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA), thyroarytenoid, and thyropharyngeus, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN), a branch of the vagus nerve.
source: Muscles of the laryngopharynx include thyrohyoid, posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA), thyroarytenoid, and thyropharyngeus, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN), a branch of the vagus nerve (Erik Van Lunteren, 1988; Nasri et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erik Van Lunteren, 1988; Nasri et al., 1997

claim: 403 ± 39 ChAT+-expressing neurons were found in the rostrocaudal distribution of PiCo.
source: First, in the rostrocaudal distribution, we found 403 ± 39 ChAT+-expressing neurons, with the most rostral portion of the denominated PiCo neurons located next to the caudal pole of the facial nucleus, extending from –6.6 to –7.3 mm from Bregma level, reaching caudally to the nucleus ambiguus (NAmb) non-compact portion (Bregma –7.3 mm).
evidence: Data from histological analysis in N=4 animals

claim: The most rostral portion of PiCo neurons is located next to the caudal pole of the facial nucleus, extending from –6.6 to –7.3 mm from Bregma level.

source: Our study confirms aspects of Toor et al., who previously hypothesized, under fictive conditions (deafferented and paralyzed), that neurons of the IRt in the PiCo area of rats act as a hub for swallow and laryngeal activity (Toor et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Toor et al., 2019

claim: Activating glutamatergic/cholinergic interneurons within the PiCo region triggered motor patterns of both swallow and laryngeal-related nerve and muscle activation, specific to respiratory phase activity.
source: We find that activating glutamatergic/cholinergic interneurons within the PiCo region triggered motor patterns of both swallow and laryngeal-related nerve and muscle activation, specific to respiratory phase activity (Figure 1).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: Swallow motor activity was evoked in an all-or-none manner, and preferentially when stimulating ChATcre:Vglut2FlpO:ChR2 neurons during inspiration.
source: Swallow motor activity was evoked in an all-or-none manner, and preferentially when stimulating ChATcre:Vglut2FlpO:ChR2 neurons during inspiration.
evidence: Data from experiments

claim: Swallow motor activity outlasted the triggering stimulus and either abruptly terminated ongoing inspiratory activity or if the stimulus did not terminate inspiration, swallowing occurred after the completion of inspiratory activity.
source: Swallow motor activity outlasted the triggering stimulus and either abruptly terminated ongoing inspiratory activity or if the stimulus did not terminate inspiration, swallowing occurred after the completion of inspiratory activity.
evidence: Data from experiments

claim: Prolonged stimulation of PiCo neurons (10 s) does not trigger sequential swallows; however, it produces one swallow at the beginning of the stimulus.
source: Prolonged stimulation of these neurons (10 s) does not trigger sequential swallows; however, it produces one swallow at the beginning of the stimulus, while inhibiting inspiration, when the stimulus occurs during or right after inspiration (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: PiCo is mutually connected with the inspiratory CPG, the preBötC.
source: As already demonstrated by Anderson et al., PiCo is mutually connected with the inspiratory CPG, the preBötC (Anderson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2016

claim: Stimulating Dbx1 neurons in the area of the preBötC inhibits ongoing activity in PiCo via GABAergic mechanisms.
source: Stimulating Dbx1 neurons in the area of the preBötC inhibits ongoing activity in PiCo via GABAergic mechanisms, while stimulating PiCo cholinergic neurons inhibits ongoing inspiratory activity and resets respiratory activity in vitro and in vivo (Anderson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2016

claim: Stimulating PiCo cholinergic neurons inhibits ongoing inspiratory activity and resets respiratory activity in vitro and in vivo.
source: Stimulating Dbx1 neurons in the area of the preBötC inhibits ongoing activity in PiCo via GABAergic mechanisms, while stimulating PiCo cholinergic neurons inhibits ongoing inspiratory activity and resets respiratory activity in vitro and in vivo (Anderson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2016

claim: PiCo functions as a gate for coordinating swallow and breathing.
source: Here, we show that PiCo functions as a gate.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: For the PiCo-mediated phase-dependent mechanism to occur, bilateral stimulation of a sufficient number of PiCo neurons is necessary.
source: However, for the PiCo-mediated phase-dependent mechanism to occur, bilateral stimulation of a sufficient number of PiCo neurons is necessary since incomplete and/or asymmetric expression of channelrhodopsin in the population of glutamatergic/cholinergic PiCo neurons led to an upper airway motor activity characterized by abnormal temporal activation and coordination between the laryngeal and submental complex (Figure 6).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 6

claim: PiCo-stimulated swallow activity was triggered in an all-or-none manner, similar to swallows evoked by liquid, brainstem, and superior laryngeal nerve (SLN) electrical stimulation.
source: PiCo-stimulated swallow activity was triggered in an all-or-none manner, similar to swallows evoked by liquid, brainstem, and superior laryngeal nerve (SLN) electrical stimulation, a concept established in the late 1800s (Meltzer, 1883; Miller and Sherrington, 1915).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meltzer, 1883; Miller and Sherrington, 1915

claim: Laryngeal activation had a graded response dependent on the duration of the optogenetic stimulus.
source: By contrast, laryngeal activation had a graded response dependent on the duration of the optogenetic stimulus (Figure 3).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 3

claim: The laryngeal activity evoked by PiCo stimulation could be a central and integral component to a laryngeal adductor reflex (LAR), an airway protective mechanism that prevents aspiration of foreign material.
source: The laryngeal activity evoked by PiCo stimulation could be a central and integral component to a laryngeal adductor reflex (LAR), an airway protective mechanism that prevents aspiration of foreign material (Kaneoka et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Kaneoka et al., 2018

claim: PiCo is involved in multiple laryngeal postinspiratory behaviors such as vocalization, LAR (laryngeal activation) and coughing.
source: As originally hypothesized by Anderson et al., we believe that PiCo is involved in multiple laryngeal postinspiratory behaviors (Anderson et al., 2016) such as vocalization (Wei et al., 2022), LAR (laryngeal activation) and coughing.
evidence: Inference supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2016 and Wei et al., 2022

claim: Inhibition of the IRt blocks fictive swallow but not swallow-related apnea generated by SLN stimulation.
source: It has been hypothesized that inhibition of the IRt blocks fictive swallow but not swallow-related apnea. We want to emphasize that this apnea was generated by SLN stimulation and not by a natural swallow stimulation (Toor et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Toor et al., 2019

claim: SLN stimulation causes endogenous release of adenosine that activates 2A receptors on GABAergic neurons, resulting in the release of GABA on inspiratory neurons and subsequent inspiratory inhibition.
source: It is known that SLN stimulation causes endogenous release of adenosine that activates 2A receptors on GABAergic neurons, resulting in the release of GABA on inspiratory neurons and subsequent inspiratory inhibition (Abu-Shaweesh, 2007), suggesting that the SLN-evoked apnea may not be the same as a swallow-related apnea.
evidence: Supported by citation to Abu-Shaweesh, 2007

claim: Microinjections of isoguvacine into the Bötzinger complex attenuated the apneic response but not the ELM burst activity.
source: Moreover, microinjections of isoguvacine into the Bötzinger complex attenuated the apneic response but not the ELM burst activity (Sun et al., 2011), suggesting that the Bötzinger complex, not PiCo, could be involved in modulating the swallow induced apnea.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2011

claim: The Bötzinger complex, not PiCo, could be involved in modulating the swallow induced apnea.
source: Moreover, microinjections of isoguvacine into the Bötzinger complex attenuated the apneic response but not the ELM burst activity (Sun et al., 2011), suggesting that the Bötzinger complex, not PiCo, could be involved in modulating the swallow induced apnea.
evidence: Inference from cited study

claim: Respiratory oscillators can modulate other orofacial premotor oscillators such as whisking and sniffing.
source: Kleinfeld and colleagues introduce the concept of pre-premotor regions 'pre2motor' to describe that respiratory oscillators can modulate other orofacial premotor oscillators such as whisking and sniffing (McElvain et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2014) and recently described swallow (Huff et al., 2022; Pitts et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to McElvain et al., 2018; Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2014

claim: By modulating the preBötzinger complex, swallow can be shifted to different times of the respiratory cycle as well as changing swallow-related amplitude, laryngeal duration, and motor pattern sequence.
source: By modulating the preBötzinger complex, swallow can be shifted to different times of the respiratory cycle as well as changing swallow-related amplitude, laryngeal duration, and motor pattern sequence (Huff et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huff et al., 2022

claim: Triggering swallow via PiCo activation results in a phase delay of the respiratory cycle, resetting the rhythm.
source: Triggering swallow via PiCo activation results in a phase delay of the respiratory cycle, resetting the rhythm, whereas laryngeal activation (non-swallow) has a weaker effect on respiration phase (Figure 2).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: Activation of PiCo-specific neurons arrested or abrogate inspiration triggering swallow, further indicating swallow's hierarchical control over breathing.
source: Activation of PiCo-specific neurons arrested or abrogate inspiration triggering swallow, further indicating swallow's hierarchical control over breathing (Figure 2C; Dick et al., 1993; Huff et al., 2022; Miller and Sherrington, 1915; Pitts et al., 2018).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 2C and supported by citations

claim: There are neuronal projections from Kölliker-Fuse and NTS to PiCo.
source: A previous study in the rat anatomically describes neuronal projections from Kölliker-Fuse and NTS to PiCo (Oliveira et al., 2021), suggesting that PiCo's involvement in swallow–breathing coordination also involves the Parabrachial Nucleus and Kölliker-Fuse Nucleus in the dorsolateral pons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliveira et al., 2021

claim: The Parabrachial Nucleus and Kölliker-Fuse Nucleus have been implicated as a sensory relay for the larynx, in particular postinspiratory activity of laryngeal adductor and swallow–breathing coordination.
source: These areas have previously been implicated as a sensory relay for the larynx, in particular postinspiratory activity of laryngeal adductor and swallow–breathing coordination (Bautista and Dutschmann, 2014; Dutschmann and Herbert, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bautista and Dutschmann, 2014; Dutschmann and Herbert, 2006

claim: Behaviorally occurring swallows in response to food or liquid have to be dynamic and alter their timing, duration, and amplitude to accommodate for change in bolus size, texture, and consistency via afferent sensory feedback mechanisms.
source: Behaviorally occurring swallows in response to food or liquid have to be dynamic and alter their timing, duration, and amplitude to accommodate for change in bolus size, texture, and consistency via afferent sensory feedback mechanisms (Dantas et al., 1990; Hrycyshyn and Basmajian, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dantas et al., 1990; Hrycyshyn and Basmajian, 1972

claim: There are known projections from NTS to PiCo and connections between PiCo and preBötC.
source: There are known projections from NTS to PiCo (Oliveira et al., 2021) and connections between PiCo and preBötC (Anderson et al., 2016), giving reason to suggest that PiCo acts as an interface between the SPG and preBötC.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oliveira et al., 2021 and Anderson et al., 2016

claim: PiCo acts as an interface between the SPG and preBötC.
source: There are known projections from NTS to PiCo (Oliveira et al., 2021) and connections between PiCo and preBötC (Anderson et al., 2016), giving reason to suggest that PiCo acts as an interface between the SPG and preBötC.
evidence: Inference from cited anatomical data

claim: PiCo-triggered swallows preserve the rostrocaudal swallow pattern and hyoid elevation seen in physiological swallows.
source: Here, we show that PiCo-triggered swallows preserve the rostrocaudal swallow pattern and hyoid elevation seen in physiological swallows (Doty and Bosma, 1956; Thexton et al., 2007), suggesting excitatory inputs between PiCo and the SPG.
evidence: Data from experiments and supported by citations to Doty and Bosma, 1956; Thexton et al., 2007

claim: PiCo-triggered swallows occur at a broader range of the respiratory cycle, while still predominantly occurring within the postinspiratory phase.
source: However, PiCo-triggered swallows occur at a broader range of the respiratory cycle, while still predominantly occurring within the postinspiratory phase (Figure 4).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Duration and amplitude of swallow-related muscle and nerve activity were decreased during PiCo-stimulated swallows compared to water-evoked swallows.
source: We also find that duration and amplitude of swallow-related muscle and nerve activity were decreased during PiCo-stimulated swallows compared to water-evoked swallows (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The differences between PiCo-triggered and water-evoked swallows are likely due to the fact that the PiCo-triggered swallows are missing the behavioral context of water-evoked swallows and do not activate the sensory component of the SPG to the same extent.
source: These differences are likely due to the fact that the PiCo-triggered swallows are missing the behavioral context of water-evoked swallows and do not activate the sensory component of the SPG to the same extent as the water-evoked swallows.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: Swallow has been thought of as an 'all-or-nothing' response as early as 1883.
source: Swallow has been thought of as an 'all-or-nothing' response as early as 1883 (Meltzer, 1883).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meltzer, 1883

claim: Whether modulating spinal or vagal feedback, central drive for swallow/breathing, or lesions in swallow related areas of the brainstem, swallow either occurred or did not.
source: Whether modulating spinal or vagal feedback (Huff et al., 2020), central drive for swallow/breathing (Huff et al., 2022), or lesions in swallow related areas of the brainstem (Jean and Car, 1979; Doty et al., 1967; Wang and Bieger, 1991), swallow either occurred or did not.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Swallows are thought to be a fixed action pattern, with duration of stimulation having no effect on behavior duration.
source: Swallows are thought to be a fixed action pattern, with duration of stimulation having no effect on behavior duration (Figure 3; Dick et al., 1993).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation to Dick et al., 1993

claim: If insufficient numbers of neurons are activated, PiCo's influence to specifically activate swallow or laryngeal activation is blurred, resulting in the uncoordinated activation of muscles involved in both behaviors.
source: Thus, if insufficient numbers of neurons are activated, PiCo's influence to specifically activate swallow or laryngeal activation is blurred, resulting in the uncoordinated activation of muscles involved in both behaviors, which does not occur in an all-or-none manner.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: It is possible that PiCo is involved in assembling the swallow motor pattern itself.
source: Thus, it is possible that PiCo is involved in assembling the swallow motor pattern itself and unilateral activation of PiCo could either desynchronize swallow interneurons or activate only one side of the SPG.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations

claim: Diaphragm activity has been shown to be multimodal, having different activity patterns for swallow and breathing, including concurrent inhibited respiratory-related activity and activated swallow-related activity, Schluckatmung, in physiological and fictive swallows.
source: Diaphragm activity has been shown to be multimodal, having different activity patterns for swallow and breathing, including concurrent inhibited respiratory-related activity and activated swallow-related activity, Schluckatmung, in physiological and fictive swallows (Huff et al., 2022; Pitts et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huff et al., 2022; Pitts et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2018

claim: Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PiCo area resulted in swallow-related diaphragmatic activation, Schluckatmung.
source: Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PiCo area resulted in swallow-related diaphragmatic activation, Schluckatmung (Figure 1C).
evidence: Data from experiments shown in Figure 1C

claim: The SPG activates pre-motor neurons in the dorsal respiratory group responsible for diaphragm recruitment during swallow.
source: It has been hypothesized that the SPG activates pre-motor neurons in the dorsal respiratory group responsible for diaphragm recruitment during swallow, and inspiratory neurons of the medial reticular formation have been shown to increase firing frequency during Schluckatmung (Pitts et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pitts et al., 2021; Pitts et al., 2018

claim: Anesthesia can decrease, and sometimes abolish, laryngeal postinspiratory activity.
source: Anesthesia can decrease, and sometimes abolish, laryngeal postinspiratory activity (Henderson-Smart et al., 1982; Sherrey and Megirian, 1974), and it can also decrease the excitability of swallow reflex (D'Angelo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Henderson-Smart et al., 1982; Sherrey and Megirian, 1974; D'Angelo et al., 2014

claim: Anesthesia can decrease the excitability of swallow reflex.
source: Anesthesia can decrease, and sometimes abolish, laryngeal postinspiratory activity (Henderson-Smart et al., 1982; Sherrey and Megirian, 1974), and it can also decrease the excitability of swallow reflex (D'Angelo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Angelo et al., 2014

claim: Injection of water into the oral cavity of a ChATcre:Ai32 and a ChATcre:Vglut2FlpO:ChR2 mouse did not evoke a swallow, which is likely due to the depth of anesthesia.
source: Here, we found that injection of water into the oral cavity of a ChATcre:Ai32 and a ChATcre:Vglut2FlpO:ChR2 mouse did not evoke a swallow, which is likely due to the depth of anesthesia.
evidence: Data from experiments and inference about anesthesia effect

claim: Opening the tracheal window disrupts the positive subglottic pressure generated during expiration, leading to lengthening of expiratory duration and irregular breathing.
source: Another limiting factor of our preparation is the need to open the tracheal window which disrupts the positive subglottic pressure generated during expiration. This leads to lengthening of expiratory duration and also causes irregular breathing (Henderson-Smart et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Henderson-Smart et al., 1982

claim: Aspiration pneumonia is the leading cause of death in neurodegenerative disease.
source: Discoordination leads to aspiration pneumonia, the leading cause of death in neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: General medical knowledge

claim: Leigh syndrome, stroke, and Parkinson's disease, as well as obstructive sleep apnea and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, all have high incidences of aspiration pneumonia.
source: Leigh syndrome, stroke, and Parkinson's disease, as well as obstructive sleep apnea and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, all have high incidences of aspiration pneumonia (Armstrong and Mosher, 2011; Cvejic and Bardin, 2018; Su et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2022; Won et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Aspiration is the result of a discoordination of laryngeal closure during swallow that allows foreign material to enter into the airway instead of the esophagus.
source: Aspiration is the result of a discoordination of laryngeal closure during swallow that allows foreign material to enter into the airway instead of the esophagus.
evidence: General medical knowledge

claim: PiCo mediates airway protective behaviors.
source: Using optogenetic approaches in freely breathing anesthetized ChATcre:Ai32, Vglut2cre:Ai32 and intersectional recombination of ChATcre:Vglut2FlpO:ChR2 mice reveals PiCo mediates airway protective behaviors.
evidence: Data from optogenetic experiments

claim: Activation of PiCo during inspiration or the beginning of postinspiration triggers swallow behavior in an all-or-nothing manner.
source: Activation of PiCo during inspiration or the beginning of postinspiration triggers swallow behavior in an all-or-nothing manner, while there is a higher probability for stimulating only laryngeal activation when activated further into expiration.
evidence: Data from optogenetic experiments

claim: There is a higher probability for stimulating only laryngeal activation when PiCo is activated further into expiration.
source: Activation of PiCo during inspiration or the beginning of postinspiration triggers swallow behavior in an all-or-nothing manner, while there is a higher probability for stimulating only laryngeal activation when activated further into expiration.
evidence: Data from optogenetic experiments

claim: Laryngeal activation is dependent on stimulation duration.
source: Laryngeal activation is dependent on stimulation duration.
evidence: Data from optogenetic experiments

claim: Sufficient bilateral PiCo activation is necessary for preserving the physiological swallow motor sequence.
source: Sufficient bilateral PiCo activation is necessary for preserving the physiological swallow motor sequence since activation of only a few PiCo neurons or unilateral activation leads to blurred upper airway behavioral responses.
evidence: Data from optogenetic experiments

claim: Activation of only a few PiCo neurons or unilateral activation leads to blurred upper airway behavioral responses.
source: Sufficient bilateral PiCo activation is necessary for preserving the physiological swallow motor sequence since activation of only a few PiCo neurons or unilateral activation leads to blurred upper airway behavioral responses.
evidence: Data from optogenetic experiments

claim: PiCo acts as an interface between the swallow pattern generator and the preBötzinger complex to coordinate swallow and breathing.
source: We believe PiCo acts as an interface between the swallow pattern generator and the preBötzinger complex to coordinate swallow and breathing.
evidence: Inference from experimental data
